hints: When the frame slides, a reading that is smaller than a newer reading to its right can never be the peak again. Why keep it?
Use a monotonic deque of indices whose readings are in decreasing order. The front is always the current frame's maximum.

1. Create an empty deque of indices.
  2. For each i: remove the front index if it is outside the frame (<= i - k).
  3. Pop from the back while the reading there is <= readings[i]; then push i.
  4. Once i >= k - 1, add readings[front] to the answer.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: For every frame position, scan its k readings for the maximum.

approaches.name: Better
approaches.idea: Keep the frame in a max-heap (or TreeMap) and lazily drop items that slid out.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Monotonic decreasing deque of indices; each index is pushed and popped at most once.

explain: For [2,-1,4,3,0,5,1] with k = 3: after the first three readings the deque holds just index 2 (value 4), because 4 pushed out 2 and -1, so the first peak is 4. Then 3 and 0 join behind it, and 4 stays the peak for two more frames. When 5 arrives, it clears everything, giving 5 for the last two frames: [4,4,4,5,5]. The deque stays decreasing, so its front is the max of the frame. Remember to drop the front when its index slides out of the frame.
recognize: Max (or min) of every fixed-size window → monotonic deque.
